section.title: A Light to the Nations
section.sectionRationale: This chapter contains the second of Isaiah's Servant Songs, verses 1 to 6, in which the Servant, called and named before birth, is told that restoring Jacob alone is too small a task, He will also be a light to the nations, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. The chapter then turns to comfort Zion directly, using the tenderest image in the whole book, a mother's love, to promise that God has not forgotten His people.
section.thesis: The Servant, called from the womb for a mission that seemed to fail, is told that His calling is too great to be limited to restoring Israel alone, He will be a light to the nations, and the LORD reassures grieving Zion that, sooner than a mother could forget her nursing child, He has not and will not forget His people.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: the Servant called and named from the womb; the climactic widening of His mission to be a light for the nations; the LORD's help in the day of salvation; a highway home through every mountain made a road; the LORD's tender reassurance that He has not forgotten Zion; the sudden gathering of returning children; foreign kings serving as caretakers; and the closing certainty that the LORD will rescue His people from even the mightiest oppressor.

units.label: The LORD called Me from the womb

verses.text: Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples: The LORD called Me from the womb; from the body of My mother He named Me.
He made My mouth like a sharp sword; He hid Me in the shadow of His hand. He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver.
He said to Me, “You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory.”
But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity; yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God.”

units.label: A light for the nations
units.note: salvation to the ends of the earth

verses.text: And now says the LORD, who formed Me from the womb to be His Servant, to bring Jacob back to Him, that Israel might be gathered to Him, for I am honored in the sight of the LORD, and My God is My strength,

He says: “It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel. I will also make You a {{or|light}} for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.”

Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, to Him who was despised and abhorred by the nation, to the Servant of rulers: “Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down, because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen You.”

units.label: In the day of salvation I will help you

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You; I will keep You and appoint You to be a covenant for the people, to restore the land, to apportion its desolate inheritances,
to say to the prisoners, ‘Come out,’ and to those in darkness, ‘Show yourselves.’ They will feed along the pathways, and find pasture on every barren hill.
They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them. For He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water.
I will turn all My mountains into roads, and My highways will be raised up.
Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan.”
Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains! For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones.

units.label: Can a woman forget her nursing child?

verses.text: But Zion said, “The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!”
“Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack {{racham|compassion}} for the son of her womb? Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!
Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me.

units.label: Lift up your eyes and look around

verses.text: Your builders hasten back; your destroyers and wreckers depart from you.
Lift up your eyes and look around. They all gather together; they come to you. As surely as I live,” declares the LORD, “you will wear them all as jewelry and put them on like a bride.
For your ruined and desolate places and your ravaged land will now indeed be too small for your people, and those who devoured you will be far away.
Yet the children of your bereavement will say in your hearing, ‘This place is too small for us; make room for us to live here.’

Then you will say in your heart, ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was bereaved and barren; I was exiled and rejected. So who has reared them? Look, I was left all alone, so where did they come from?’”

units.label: Kings will be your foster fathers

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will lift up My hand to the nations, and raise My banner to the peoples. They will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders.

Kings will be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. They will bow to you facedown and lick the dust at your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who hope in Me will never be put to shame.”

units.label: Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty?
units.note: all flesh will know their Savior

verses.text: Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?

Indeed, this is what the LORD says: “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved; I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.

I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh; they will be drunk on their own blood, as with wine. Then all mankind will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.”

or.gloss: Light, the very first thing God calls into being in Genesis 1:3. To be made a light for the nations is to be given the highest possible calling, bringing not merely information but salvation itself to peoples far beyond Israel, a mission the New Testament identifies as fulfilled and continued in Christ and His church.

racham.gloss: Compassion, tender mercy, a word built on the same root as rechem, womb, so that a mother's compassion for the child of her own body becomes the very picture Scripture reaches for to describe God's love. Even this deepest human bond, the LORD insists, is a weaker analogy than His own unforgettable commitment to His people.

basic.context: This chapter contains the second Servant Song, where a figure called and named before birth confesses that His labor has felt like failure, yet is told that His mission is actually too great to be limited to restoring Israel, He will be a light to the nations, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. The chapter then turns to comfort a grieving Zion, who feels forgotten, with the tenderest image available: a mother's love for her own nursing child.
basic.hermeneutics: The Servant is called 'Israel' in verse 3 yet is given a mission to Israel in verses 5 to 6, restoring Jacob and gathering Israel, a tension resolved when the Servant is understood to represent and embody Israel's true calling even while personally distinct from the nation, succeeding at the very vocation Israel as a whole had failed. This reading is confirmed directly when Paul and Barnabas apply verse 6 to their own Gentile mission grounded in Christ, Acts 13:47.
basic.originalLanguages: The Servant's mission climaxes in being made an {{or}}, light, for the nations, the highest possible calling, bringing salvation itself to the ends of the earth. Zion's despair is answered by an appeal to {{racham}}, compassion, the tender mercy a mother feels for the child of her own womb, which the LORD says is a weaker bond than His own unbreakable commitment to His people.
basic.typology: The Servant called and named from the womb, whose labor initially seems futile yet is vindicated and expanded into a mission to the whole earth, anticipates Christ's own path through apparent failure at the cross to global, resurrection-vindicated triumph. The image of Zion's children being restored to her, more numerous than she can hold, anticipates the growth of the church gathered from every nation.
basic.christ: Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6 directly, declaring, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth,' and apply this Servant's mission to their own gospel preaching, grounded in Christ, Acts 13:47. Simeon likewise recognizes the infant Jesus as 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:32, directly echoing this Servant Song. The Servant's confession, 'I have labored in vain,' verse 4, anticipates and is answered by Christ's resurrection, which vindicated what looked, at the cross, like total failure.
basic.god: God calls and names His Servant before birth for a purpose far greater than first appears, and He does not abandon that purpose even when it seems to fail. He is also the God whose compassion for His people exceeds even a mother's love for her nursing child, a bond He Himself created as merely a faint echo of His own unbreakable commitment.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 13:47 quotes Isaiah 49:6 directly, applying the Servant's mission of light to the nations to the apostolic proclamation of Christ. Luke 2:32 has Simeon recognize the infant Jesus as this very light for revelation to the Gentiles. John 10:28-29 echoes the promise that no one can snatch God's people from His hand. Matthew 2:15 applies similar Israel-and-Servant typology, quoting Hosea 11:1 of the infant Jesus.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's Servant, whose apparent failure becomes the platform for a mission to the whole earth, and its picture of a God whose compassion exceeds even a mother's love, traces the whole Bible's pattern of purpose vindicated through weakness and love that will not let go. It anticipates Christ, the true Light to the nations, who was despised yet is now exalted, gathering children for God from every corner of the earth.

context.literary:
Isaiah 49 opens a new movement in the book. Until now the Servant has mostly been spoken about, as in Isaiah 42:1-4, and here, for the first time, he speaks for himself, and he does so to an audience far beyond Israel: 'Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples.' This is the second of the four Servant Songs, which run through Isaiah 42:1-4, 49:1-6, 50:4-9 and 52:13 to 53:12, and it is the one in which the Servant's own inner life is heard most openly.

The chapter divides into two large halves joined by a hymn. Verses 1 to 6 are the Servant's account of his calling, in a five step order: called and named before birth, verse 1; equipped as a sword and an arrow, verse 2; addressed as 'Israel,' verse 3; discouraged, verse 4; and recommissioned on a larger scale, verses 5 and 6. Verses 7 to 12 turn to promise, with an oracle to the despised Servant followed by a vision of captives set free and led home along raised highways. Verse 13 is a call for heaven and earth to sing, and verses 14 to 26 form the second half, which answers the complaint of Zion.

Both halves move on the same rhythm of complaint and answer. The Servant says he has laboured in vain, verse 4, and is told that his work is too small, verse 6. Zion says she has been forsaken and forgotten, verse 14, and is told that she cannot be forgotten, verse 15. After each answer the promise grows beyond what the speaker had imagined. The Servant asks for vindication and receives the nations; Zion asks to be remembered and receives more children than she can house.

The womb and the mother run through the chapter, in verses 1, 5 and 15 and again in the bereaved mother of verse 21, and they give it a unity of image. The Servant is called from the womb and Zion is compared to a mother whose womb has been emptied and then filled.
context.historical:
The chapter speaks to Judeans who feel that the story is over. Lamentations records their mood: 'Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?' Lamentations 5:20. Isaiah 49:14 repeats the very complaint, using the same two verbs of forgetting and forsaking. An exiled people had lost their city, their temple, their king and any visible sign of favour. They thought of themselves as bereaved, barren and alone, as verse 21 says. In the ancient world a woman without children was often regarded as without a future, and the image would have hit with real force.

The geography in verses 11 and 12 is also telling. The returning people will come from the north, the west and 'the land of Aswan,' a region in southern Egypt, which is the reading of the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Hebrew in the traditional text is Sinim, whose location is uncertain. Jewish communities lived in southern Egypt in the Persian period, notably on the island of Elephantine at Aswan, so the reference fits what is known of the dispersion. The point is that the scattering was wide and that no exile is too far for the promise.

The images of kings serving as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers, verse 23, belong to the world of royal patronage. Persian rulers did in fact give resources for the rebuilding of the temple, Ezra 1:1-4, and a later Persian king allowed the walls to be rebuilt. Isaiah's language is bolder than any of that, since it looks to a day when the rulers of the nations will bow, and the passage should be read as a prophecy that goes beyond the first return.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 49:1-6 is the pivot of the Servant Songs. The Servant of Isaiah 42:1-4 brings justice to the nations and is a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6, and the second song takes up the same vocation in the first person. The third song, Isaiah 50:4-9, adds the Servant's obedience and suffering, and the fourth, Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, completes the picture with his death and exaltation. The words 'despised and abhorred' in verse 7 prepare for 'despised and rejected' in Isaiah 53:3, and the kings who rise and bow in verse 7 anticipate the kings who 'shut their mouths because of Him' in Isaiah 52:15.

The chapter also looks back. The call from the womb recalls Jeremiah, to whom God said 'before you were born I set you apart,' Jeremiah 1:5, and the sword in the mouth and the shadow of the hand return in Isaiah 51:16. The mission to the nations carries forward the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3.

The New Testament quotes the chapter directly. Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles at Antioch with the words of verse 6, Acts 13:47. Paul describes his own call in the language of the Servant, for God 'set me apart from my mother's womb,' Galatians 1:15, and he cites verse 8 as the day of salvation that has come, 2 Corinthians 6:2. Revelation 7:16-17 takes the promise of verse 10, that they will not hunger or thirst, and fulfils it in the multitude before the throne. Simeon takes up the light for the nations in Luke 2:32, and Jesus' word about drawing everyone to Himself, John 12:32, belongs to the same horizon.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet writes to people who are tired. The Servant's speech in verse 4 is the most honest line in the chapter: 'I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity.' It is placed in the middle of a calling and a promise, and it shows that the one chosen for the largest task knows what it is to feel that nothing is working. Isaiah's first hearers were drained and nothing in their circumstances said otherwise. The chapter gives them permission to say so, and then it sets their weariness inside a plan that is greater than they could see.

The second aim is to enlarge their sense of purpose. Verse 6 is the surprise of the chapter. The Servant is told that to raise up Jacob is not enough. The calling of Israel was never meant to end with Israel, and their rescue from Babylon is a first step toward the rescue of the nations. Israel had been called to be a light, a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:5-6, and the exile made them forget it. Isaiah puts the vocation back in front of them.

The third aim is to answer the grief of Zion. Verses 14 to 26 are for those who think God has forgotten. The prophet's reply is not an argument but a picture, a mother and her nursing child, followed by a more personal picture still, the name engraved on a hand. His intention is to settle the question of whether God remembers, so that the exiles can begin to look up and count the children who are coming home.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The Servant's story is described, not prescribed. The call from the womb, the labour in vain, the vindication and the larger mission are things the text says of this particular Servant, and the New Testament reads them first of Christ. Readers should be careful not to treat the passage as a general promise that every effort will turn out to be secretly successful. The Servant says 'My vindication is with the LORD' and trusts that it will come. He does not say it has arrived, and the passage does not guarantee that the results of any ministry will be visible in a believer's lifetime.\n\nThe command that does carry forward is in Acts 13:47, where Paul and Barnabas say that the Lord has commanded them to bring light to the Gentiles, quoting this verse. The apostles read the Servant's mission as something that the church shares, with Christ as the light and the church as those who carry it. That is a warrant for mission and not for pride. The language of kings who bow and 'lick the dust' in verse 23 is the poetry of a reversal of fortunes, not an instruction to expect political dominance. The mother image describes God's compassion without making a claim about God's gender, and the engraving on the palms is a figure for being permanently in His care, not a description of a physical mark.

debates.question: Why is the Servant called 'Israel' in verse 3 when He is also given a mission to Israel in verses 5 and 6?

views.label: The Servant is the nation Israel
views.case: The text says 'You are My Servant, Israel,' and Isaiah 41:8 and 44:1 call the nation 'My servant.' On this reading verses 5 and 6 distinguish between Israel as a whole and the faithful part of Israel who are to restore the rest, so that the Servant is the believing core of the nation or the nation in its ideal calling.

views.label: An individual who embodies Israel
views.case: The Servant has a mother, a womb, a mouth and a personal sense of failure, and he is sent to bring Jacob back to Him, which is hard to say of Jacob himself. On this view the Servant is one person who stands for the nation and who succeeds where the nation failed, as the New Testament says of Jesus when it applies to Him a text about the nation, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15.

views.label: The prophet as a representative
views.case: Some interpreters read the voice as that of the prophet who has laboured among a resistant people and who sees himself as embodying Israel's calling. Isaiah 50:10 speaks of obeying the voice of the Servant, which could fit a prophet. They then see the New Testament as applying the pattern to Christ in a fuller way.

debates.bearing: The three readings are not as far apart as they look. The calling is Israel's, the one who carries it out is an individual, and he does so as Israel's representative. The New Testament's reading of this song of Christ, Luke 2:32 and Acts 13:47, follows the second view, and it does not deny the first, since Jesus is the true Israel who does what Israel did not.

debates.question: Whose captives are recovered in verse 24, and who are the 'tyrant' and 'the mighty'?

views.label: The captives of a tyrant
views.case: The BSB follows the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Syriac and the Vulgate, which read 'the captives of a tyrant,' and this fits the parallel line about 'the mighty' and the answer of verse 25, 'the captives of the mighty will be taken away.' The question is whether the oppressed can really be set free from a strong captor, and the answer is that they can.

views.label: The captives of the righteous
views.case: The traditional Hebrew text reads 'the captives of the righteous,' which is difficult. Some take it as 'rightful captives,' people justly held, as the exiles were, since God had given them into Babylon's hand. The question then becomes whether even justly taken captives can be released, and the answer is that God will do it for His own sake.

debates.bearing: Either way, verse 25 gives the same answer. Captives of the mighty will be taken away, and God Himself will contend with those who contend with Zion. The textual difference matters for how we read the question, but the content of the promise is stable, that God is stronger than the one who holds His people.

study.originalLanguages:
The most striking word in the Servant's complaint is the one translated 'futility' in verse 4, tohu. It is the word used in Genesis 1:2 for the earth 'formless' before God ordered it. In Isaiah it is used of the idol makers who are 'nothing,' Isaiah 44:9, and of the earth that God did not create 'to be empty,' Isaiah 45:18. The Servant's own sense of emptiness therefore borrows the vocabulary of chaos, and he says that his work has returned to the void. The answer is that the God who did not create the earth for emptiness will not let His Servant's labour be empty. The Servant adds that his 'vindication' is with the LORD, which is literally 'my justice,' and that his 'reward' is with his God, a word that means the wage of work. He appeals to a righteous judge for payment.

The pivotal phrase of verse 6 is built on the verb for 'be light.' The sentence runs 'It is too light a thing that You should be My Servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob.' The BSB renders it 'It is not enough,' and the sense is that the task is too small, not too hard. The mission has to be bigger to be worthy of the one who is sent. The title 'a light for the nations' appears also in Isaiah 42:6, where it is joined to 'a covenant for the people,' and the same two titles appear again in verse 8. The Servant is not only one who brings a covenant but a person who is the covenant. The word for 'nations' is goyim, the word usually used for Gentiles.

Verse 1 addresses the 'islands,' a word that the BSB footnote says can also be 'coastlands.' It means the distant lands across the sea, the far edge of the known world, and the same word is used of those who wait for the Servant's teaching in Isaiah 42:4. In verse 2 the Servant's mouth is a sharp sword and he himself a polished arrow hidden in a quiver. These are images of a word that wounds and that is held back until the moment of release. Isaiah 51:16 uses the language of words in the mouth and the shadow of the hand again, and Revelation 1:16 gives the risen Christ a sword from His mouth.

In verses 14 and 15 the same verb of forgetting appears in Zion's complaint and in God's reply. Zion says 'the Lord has forgotten me' and God says that a mother may forget, 'I will not forget you.' The answer takes the very word of the complaint and denies it. The word for 'compassion' in verse 15 is related to the Hebrew word for womb, rechem, so the compassion of a mother is a womb-love, a bond that is bodily as well as emotional. Verse 16 says 'I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands,' using the verb chaqaq, to engrave or cut in. The word 'ever before Me' is tamid, the word for what is continual, as of the regular lamp or offering in the sanctuary.

Verse 8 contains the phrase 'time of favor,' and the BSB footnote notes that the Greek Old Testament reads 'I heard You' where the Hebrew has 'I will answer You.' Paul quotes it in 2 Corinthians 6:2 in this form and declares that the time of favor has arrived.

typology.type: The Servant called from the womb and hidden in the quiver
typology.fulfillment: The Servant says that the LORD named him before birth and hid him until the right moment. The pattern is carried by the gospel record of Christ's birth announcement, Matthew 1:21, and of the long years before His public ministry, when 'His hour had not yet come,' John 7:30. Paul's own sense of being 'set apart from my mother's womb,' Galatians 1:15, uses the same language for the apostle's calling to the Gentiles. The escalation is that Christ is not only called before birth but is the eternal Son. The type is limited because the Servant is hidden for the sake of a mission, while Christ is the eternal Son before any call was spoken.

Simeon holds the infant Jesus and calls Him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel,' Luke 2:32, echoing Isaiah 49:6. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. Paul tells King Agrippa that the Christ would 'proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles,' Acts 26:23. The escalation is from a promise about a Servant to the appearance of a person who is light. The type falls short because Israel as a nation was to be a light and failed, and the full light came in one person who is also God's own presence.

typology.type: The despised Servant before whom kings bow
typology.fulfillment: Verse 7 pictures one 'despised and abhorred by the nation' before whom kings rise and princes bow. Isaiah 53:3 repeats the contempt, and Philippians 2:9-11 describes the reversal in which God exalts the humbled Jesus so that every knee bows. The pattern of humiliation followed by universal homage is carried out in the cross and the resurrection. The type is limited because Isaiah describes a reversal of status, and the New Testament shows that the humiliation was itself the means of the victory.

typology.type: Zion's barren womb and her many children
typology.fulfillment: Zion says she was bereaved and barren, and then she finds herself surrounded by children she did not bear. Paul quotes a later chapter's version of this image, 'Rejoice, O barren woman,' Isaiah 54:1, and says that 'the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother,' Galatians 4:26-27. The children are those gathered from every nation, and the church is the fulfilment of the promise. The type is partial in that the first return from exile brought back some children, while the fullness of the promise includes the Gentiles who are brought in.

typology.type: Water and pasture for those who come home
typology.fulfillment: Verses 9 and 10 promise that the returning captives will not hunger or thirst, and that the sun will not strike them. Revelation 7:16-17 takes these words and applies them to the great crowd before the throne, with the Lamb as their shepherd leading them to springs of living water. The pattern moves from a road home through a desert to a final rest in God's presence. The type falls short because the journey from Babylon ended in a rebuilt city that still had its troubles, while the Lamb's shepherding ends in a place where God wipes every tear.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ in the most direct way of any in this part of Isaiah, because the New Testament itself uses it as a window onto His person. Simeon, holding the infant, says that he has seen God's salvation, 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel,' Luke 2:29-32. Paul and Barnabas explain their turn to the Gentiles by quoting verse 6 as a command from the Lord, Acts 13:46-47. Paul tells Agrippa that the Christ would suffer, rise and 'proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles,' Acts 26:22-23. Each of these assumes that the Servant of the second song is Jesus, and the light is the light that He is, John 8:12.

The chapter leads to Christ through the shape of the Servant's experience. The Servant is called before birth, equipped with a word like a sword, and hidden until the right moment. The Gospels trace the same course from a birth announced by an angel to the years of obscurity at Nazareth, to the sharp word of the Sermon on the Mount and the sword that comes from the mouth of the risen Lord, Revelation 1:16. The Servant's cry, 'I have labored in vain,' belongs to the same family as the cry of Psalm 22:1, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' and the rest of the Servant's story, with vindication in the hand of God, is the resurrection. The cross looks like vanity, and Easter is the vindication.

The widening of the mission in verse 6 is Christ's mission. Jesus draws everyone to Himself when He is lifted up, John 12:32, and He sends the disciples to all nations, Matthew 28:18-20. Paul says that Christ became a servant of the circumcised to confirm the promises to the fathers and 'so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy,' Romans 15:8-9. The sentence 'It is not enough' belongs to the logic of the gospel, in which no one is outside the reach of the Servant's work.

The chapter also leads to Him by the mother's love. Jesus says of Jerusalem, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' Matthew 23:37. The compassion He shows is the compassion of God in verse 15. The statement that the LORD has engraved Zion on the palms of His hands invites a gentle, but not forced, thought of the hands that Thomas was asked to look at, John 20:27. The New Testament does not make that link itself, and it should be taken as a pastoral echo and not a proof. The sure link is that the God who will not forget His people has shown it in the person of the Servant who bore the punishment that brought peace, Isaiah 53:5.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who plans before the person exists. The Servant is called from the womb and named from his mother's body, and that is a kind of knowing that comes before any action. Psalm 139:16 says of the individual that all his days were written before one of them came to be, and Isaiah 49 gives the same truth in the form of a vocation. God does not recruit as needs arise; He decides ahead, shapes and hides, and then brings out at the right time.

It shows a God who allows His servants to say the hard thing. The Servant's complaint is not rebuked. It is recorded, answered and then extended. Zion's accusation, 'The LORD has forsaken me,' is given a full reply. This is a God who permits lament, who will take the charge that He has forgotten and respond to it, and who prefers honest speech to polite silence. A reader who has said something similar to Him can take courage that the words are in the Bible.

It shows a God of compassion beyond human compassion. The comparison to a nursing mother is meant to pick the strongest tie in human life and to say that God's tie is stronger still. The phrase 'Even if she could forget' admits the shocking possibility that some mothers do, and says that God does not. It is a covenant faithfulness expressed in the language of the nursery, and it fits with Isaiah 66:13, 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you.' The engraving on the hands says that the commitment is permanent.

It shows a God who is universal in aim and particular in method. He calls one Servant, one people and one city, and He does it so that salvation will reach the ends of the earth. Verse 26 says that all mankind will know Him as Savior and Redeemer, and He is also the Mighty One of Jacob, the God of a particular family. The particular and the universal are not in competition. The line of promise has always been narrow in order to be wide.

It shows a God who is stronger than the strong. The question of verse 24, whether plunder can be taken from a mighty man, is answered with a flat yes. Tyrants have a limit, and God Himself will fight those who fight His people. For worship this means that God's people can sing in the middle of the desert, because the God who calls them from the womb will keep them to the end, and nothing, as Paul says, can separate us from His love, Romans 8:35-39.

crossReferences.note: The first Servant Song calls the Servant a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, in language that Isaiah 49:6 and 49:8 take up again. Reading the two together shows that the second song continues one vocation in which the Servant brings both justice and light to the nations.

The third song continues the Servant's own voice. He has the tongue of a disciple and a face set like flint, and he offers his back to those who strike him. It fills in what the 'labor in vain' of 49:4 begins, showing that the Servant's weariness will lead to suffering that is chosen and not merely endured.

The Servant 'despised and rejected by men' fulfils the oracle to Him who was 'despised and abhorred by the nation' in 49:7. Between the two passages the contempt is taken further, from social rejection to the full weight of suffering, and the reversal in 52:13-15 echoes the bowing of kings.

God tells Jeremiah that He knew and set him apart before he was born, and appointed him a prophet to the nations. The phrase is a close parallel to Isaiah 49:1, and it shows that the call from the womb was a recognised pattern for those with a mission to the nations, which Paul also applies to himself.

Paul and Barnabas, turned away by some of their own people, say that the Lord has commanded them to be 'a light for the Gentiles' and quote Isaiah 49:6. It shows the church taking up the Servant's mission, and it is a model of how the apostles read Isaiah.

Simeon says that his eyes have seen the salvation prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for Israel. He draws the two halves of Isaiah 49:6 together in the child, so the Gospel opens with this Servant Song fulfilled.

Paul quotes the Greek form of Isaiah 49:8, 'In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you,' and says, 'now is the time of favor.' The apostle reads the prophecy's day as having arrived with Christ, which makes the Servant's vindication a present reality.

The multitude before the throne will never hunger or thirst, and the Lamb will be their shepherd, leading them to springs of living water. This takes up Isaiah 49:10 and shows its final form, so that the road home through the desert ends at the throne of God.

The vision of Isaiah 49:22-23 returns with more detail. Ships bring the children from afar, foreigners rebuild the walls, and the sons of oppressors bow down and call Zion the City of the LORD. It shows that the promise of the nations coming to Zion is a lasting theme of the book.

Paul says that the Jerusalem above is free and is our mother, and quotes the song of the barren woman from Isaiah 54:1. He reads the many children of the once desolate Zion, from chapter 49 and its sequel, as the church that includes Jew and Gentile alike.

'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you.' The maternal image of Isaiah 49:15 returns at the end of the book. It shows that the picture of God's tender care was not a passing figure but a permanent part of Isaiah's portrait of God.

All the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. The Servant's commission to be a light to the nations is the long fulfilment of this promise. Israel's mission was always meant to reach the whole earth, and the Servant is the one who finally brings it about.

study.oneStory:
The chapter stands at the point where the Bible's story must decide whether Israel's failure is the end. God had called Abraham so that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and had called Israel at Sinai to be a kingdom of priests among all the nations, Exodus 19:5-6. By the time of the exile it looked as if both promises had gone into the ground. Isaiah 49 says that they have not. A Servant will do what the nation did not, and he will do it on a bigger stage than anyone had thought.

This is why the second Servant Song is such a hinge. It shows that the rescue of Israel and the blessing of the nations are one rescue and not two. The Servant must restore Jacob, and in restoring Jacob he becomes a light to the nations. The pattern continues through the rest of the book, in the exaltation of Isaiah 52:13-15, in the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD in Isaiah 56:6-8, and in the vision of Isaiah 60. In the Gospels the pattern is found in the person of Jesus, who is the light of the world, and in the Acts, where the light goes out from Jerusalem 'to the ends of the earth,' Acts 1:8.

The chapter also answers the grief that runs from the Garden onward. Humanity has been scattered, bereaved and exiled since Genesis 3, and Zion's cry of being forgotten gathers up that long ache. God's answer in verse 15 is that He is the one who remembers, and the whole story is an act of remembering, from Noah to the exodus to the cross. When Zion looks up and sees her children coming from every direction, the story's hope is already in view.

The ending comes in the book of Revelation. The kings of the earth bring their glory into the city whose gates are never shut, Revelation 21:24-26, which is the fullest fulfilment of the kings and nations of Isaiah 49:22-23. The Lamb shepherds the multitude to the springs of living water, Revelation 7:17, as Isaiah 49:10 promised. The mother's question 'Who has begotten these for me?' is answered by a people from every nation who have been gathered by the Servant's cost. The one who laboured in vain sees the fruit and is satisfied, Isaiah 53:11.

quiz.q: What confession does the Servant make in verse 4 despite His high calling?

options.text: That He has labored in vain and spent His strength in futility, yet trusts His vindication is with the LORD.
options.note: Verse 4 records exactly this honest confession alongside continued trust in God.

options.text: That His mission has been an unqualified, visible success from the start.
options.note: The opposite; the Servant candidly confesses a sense of futility and failure.

options.text: That He no longer trusts God at all.
options.note: Despite the sense of futility, the Servant explicitly states His vindication and reward remain with the LORD.

options.text: That He was never truly called by God in the first place.
options.note: The Servant's confession assumes and reaffirms His calling; His concern is the apparent fruit of His labor, not the reality of His calling.

quiz.q: What does the LORD say is 'not enough' for the Servant's mission in verse 6?

options.text: Restoring Jacob and the tribes of Israel alone; He will also be a light to the nations.
options.note: Verse 6 states this expansion of mission directly.

options.text: Saving anyone at all, since the mission is declared impossible.
options.note: The opposite; the verse expands rather than cancels the Servant's saving mission.

options.text: Speaking to kings and princes, since only common people matter.
options.note: Verse 7 actually describes kings rising and princes bowing, not an exclusion of rulers from the mission's scope.

options.text: Working through prophets, since only priests may act.
options.note: The passage does not distinguish between prophets and priests; it expands the Servant's mission to encompass the nations broadly.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply Isaiah 49:6?

options.text: Paul and Barnabas quote it directly as grounds for their mission bringing salvation to the Gentiles.
options.note: Acts 13:47 quotes this verse directly and applies it to the apostolic gospel mission.

options.text: It is never referenced anywhere in the New Testament.
options.note: The opposite; it is quoted directly in Acts 13:47 and echoed in Luke 2:32.

options.text: It is applied only to a future, entirely unrelated event with no Gentile mission connection.
options.note: Its clearest New Testament use directly connects it to the Gentile mission grounded in Christ.

options.text: It is used to argue against including Gentiles in salvation.
options.note: The opposite; it is used specifically to justify and ground the inclusion of Gentiles in the gospel mission.

quiz.q: What image does the LORD use in verse 15 to reassure grieving Zion?

options.text: A mother's inability to forget her own nursing child, though God's love exceeds even that.
options.note: Verse 15 uses exactly this image, then surpasses it with God's unbreakable commitment.

options.text: A soldier's duty to his commanding officer.
options.note: The image used is maternal love and compassion, not military duty.

options.text: A business contract between two merchants.
options.note: The passage uses intimate, familial imagery, not transactional business language.

options.text: A king's obligation to his most distant subjects.
options.note: The specific image given is a mother's bond with her nursing child, a far more intimate picture than a king's general obligations.

quiz.q: What certainty does the LORD express in verses 24 to 26 regarding Israel's rescue?

options.text: Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, for the LORD Himself will contend with their oppressors.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 state this certainty directly, that the LORD will rescue even from the mightiest tyrant.

options.text: Israel's rescue is uncertain and depends entirely on human military strength.
options.note: The opposite; the passage grounds the certainty of rescue in the LORD's own action, not human military might.

options.text: Only the wealthy among the captives will be rescued.
options.note: The promise is given broadly to God's people and their children, not selectively to the wealthy.

options.text: Rescue will occur, but only after many centuries of continued captivity.
options.note: The passage emphasizes the LORD's active, certain intervention, not an indefinite, centuries-long delay.

questions: The Servant confesses His labor felt like failure, yet trusts His vindication is with the LORD. Where does your own work or ministry feel fruitless right now, and how might you need to entrust the outcome to God rather than your own sense of success?
The Servant's mission was expanded far beyond what seemed 'enough,' restoring Israel, to being a light to the whole world. Where might God be calling you to a bigger vision than you have settled for?
Zion felt forgotten by God even while He carried her on the palms of His hands. When have you felt forgotten by God in a season that, looking back, you can now see He was present in all along?
God's compassion is compared to, and said to exceed, a mother's love for her nursing child. How does picturing God's love in this tender, maternal way change how you approach Him today?

The chapter closes with certainty that God will rescue His people even from the mightiest oppressor. What situation in your life feels too powerful or entrenched to change, and how might this promise reshape your prayers about it?

translationNotes.note: This is the second of Isaiah's four Servant Songs, directly quoted in Acts 13:47 and echoed in Luke 2:32 regarding the mission of light to the nations.

The Servant is called 'Israel' here even while being given a mission to restore Israel in the following verses, a tension most naturally resolved by understanding the Servant as embodying and fulfilling Israel's true vocation representatively.
The land of Aswan, sometimes rendered Sinim in other translations, likely refers to a distant southern region, emphasizing that the returning exiles will come from every direction, however far.
